stem: A patient presents to the ER after a blunt injury to the chest with hypotension, dilated neck veins and muffled heart sounds. What is the next step in management?
expl: Hypotension + distended neck veins + muffled heart sounds = Beck's triad → cardiac tamponade → pericardiocentesis (as a bridge; definitive is surgical — pericardial window/thoracotomy).

why.A: A chest tube is for haemothorax/pneumothorax.
why.B: Needle thoracostomy is for tension pneumothorax (absent breath sounds, tracheal shift).
why.D: Echo/FAST confirms, but the unstable patient needs decompression.

stem: What is the most injured organ in abdominal blunt injuries?
expl: The spleen is the most commonly injured organ in blunt abdominal trauma (liver is close second, and the commonest in penetrating trauma).

why.A: Second in blunt trauma (most common in penetrating).

stem: Which of the following organs is most commonly injured in blunt abdominal trauma?
expl: The spleen is the most commonly injured organ in blunt abdominal trauma (the liver in penetrating trauma, and in some series overall).

why.A: The diaphragm is less often injured.
why.B: The kidney is less often injured.
why.D: Small bowel is more typical of seatbelt/penetrating injury.

stem: A pregnant lady presented after a MVA. She was found to have a massive bleed but was clinically stable. What is the reason behind her stability?
expl: In pregnancy blood volume (~40–50%), stroke volume and cardiac output rise, so a pregnant woman can lose 30–35% of her volume before showing shock (the fetus may already be compromised).

why.C: Red cell mass increases too (less than plasma — physiological anaemia).

stem: A patient presents with a liver laceration of 2cm. What is the grade of the injury?
expl: AAST liver injury: grade I laceration < 1 cm deep; grade II 1–3 cm deep (≤ 10 cm long); grade III > 3 cm.

why.D: The depth is enough to grade.

stem: A patient presents to the ER after a penetrating chest injury. He has a tracheal deviation to the left side with hyperresonance and absent breath sounds in the right hemithorax. What is management?

opts.t: Chest tube without needle decompression on the left side
Needle decompression in the second intercostal space mid clavicular line on the left side
Needle decompression in the second intercostal space mid clavicular line on the right side

expl: Tracheal deviation AWAY from the right side + right hyperresonance and absent breath sounds = right tension pneumothorax → immediate needle decompression on the RIGHT (2nd ICS MCL), then chest tube. No X-ray first.

why.D: Never wait for a CXR in tension pneumothorax.

stem: What is the fluid of choice for a hypovolemic patient?
expl: Hypovolemia → isotonic crystalloid (0.9% NaCl or Ringer's lactate) expands ECF. Hypotonic fluids and D5W go into cells.

stem: A patient presents to the ER after a motor vehicle accident (MVA) with hypotension and a distended abdomen. Your trauma team is now finishing resuscitation. What is the next step in management?

opts.t: Focused assessment with sonography for trauma (FAST)

srcNote: Source key was A; corrected — see explanation. or C not sure
expl: Resuscitation is already being completed; the next step to find the source in a hypotensive patient with a distended abdomen is FAST (adjunct to the primary survey). Positive FAST + persistent instability → laparotomy. The source keyed fluids ("or C, not sure").

why.B: Laparotomy follows a positive FAST in an unstable patient.
why.D: CT is only for stable patients.

stem: A trauma patient presented with tachycardia, deviated trachea to left side, absent breath sounds on right side and JVD (typical tension pneumothorax presentation) what type of shock does the patient have?
expl: Tension pneumothorax raises intrathoracic pressure, kinks the great veins and blocks venous return → obstructive shock.

why.B: The heart pumps normally; filling is blocked.
why.D: Volume isn't lost; return is obstructed.

stem: A 10-year-old boy falls off his bicycle and hits his abdomen. Since the accident, he has been vomiting and refusing to eat. A CT scan reveals a localized intestinal hematoma. He is hemodynamically stable. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
expl: A duodenal haematoma (handlebar injury) in a stable child usually resolves with conservative care — NPO, NG decompression and nutrition (TPN if prolonged); surgery only if it fails to resolve after ~2 weeks or perforation.

why.A: Laparotomy isn't needed for a haematoma.

stem: A 28-year-old man presents to the emergency department after a minor fall. He is hemodynamically stable with mild shortness of breath. Chest X-ray reveals a mild pneumothorax, What is the most appropriate management?

opts.t: Needle decompression followed by chest tube

expl: A small traumatic pneumothorax in a stable, minimally symptomatic patient can be observed with oxygen (speeds absorption) and a repeat X-ray; a chest tube if it enlarges or the patient needs ventilation/transfer.

why.B: Not needed for a small stable pneumothorax.

stem: A 25-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with severe trauma and ongoing hemorrhage. He is hemodynamically unstable despite initial fluid resuscitation. The team decides to initiate a massive transfusion protocol. What is the recommended ratio of blood products for resuscitation in this setting? (packed red blood cells : plasma : platelets)
expl: Massive transfusion protocols give balanced products PRBC : plasma : platelets 1 : 1 : 1 to prevent dilutional coagulopathy.

stem: A 56-year-old man is in the ICU after major abdominal trauma and massive fluid resuscitation. He is hemodynamically stable but develops progressive abdominal distension, decreased urine output, and increasing ventilatory pressures. Measurement of intra-abdominal pressure shows a value of 32 mmHg. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Intra-abdominal pressure >20 mmHg with new organ dysfunction (oliguria, rising airway pressures) = abdominal compartment syndrome (32 mmHg here, after massive resuscitation).

why.B: Possible cause, but the diagnosis is ACS.

stem: A 25-year-old man arrives at the emergency department after a gunshot wound to the abdomen. He is hemodynamically unstable, with tachycardia, hypotension, and a rigid abdomen. What is the most appropriate next step?

opts.t: Focused assessment with sonography for trauma (FAST) only

expl: Gunshot wound to the abdomen with shock and peritonitis → emergency laparotomy; no imaging.

why.B: FAST adds nothing — the decision is made.

stem: A 50-year-old man arrives at the emergency department via EMS. He is pulseless on arrival. EMS reports that he had a pulse 5 minutes ago. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

opts.t: Give IV fluids and observe for return of spontaneous circulation
Perform CPR but avoid invasive measures

expl: Keyed emergency thoracotomy (written "thoracostomy"): resuscitative (ED) thoracotomy is indicated when signs of life were lost recently — penetrating < 15 min, blunt < 10 min of CPR — to release tamponade, control bleeding and clamp the aorta.

why.B: CPR alone is futile in traumatic arrest from haemorrhage/tamponade.
why.C: He had a pulse 5 minutes ago — not yet.

stem: A patient presents after penetrating trauma to the extremity. On examination, which of the following findings is considered a hard sign of vascular injury, requiring emergent surgical exploration?
expl: Hard signs of vascular injury: pulsatile bleeding, expanding haematoma, palpable thrill/audible bruit, absent pulses with ischaemia → surgery without further imaging.

why.A: A stable haematoma is a soft sign.
why.B: An absent pulse alone is debated, but pulsatile bleeding/expanding haematoma is the classic hard sign.
why.D: A nerve deficit is a soft sign.

stem: A patient admitted for elective surgery suddenly develops shock and becomes confused, requiring emergency surgical intervention. There is no available family member or contact to provide consent. What is the most appropriate course of action?

opts.t: Continue trying to find a family member
Perform the surgery immediately because it is an emergency
Delay surgery until consent is obtained

expl: Life-threatening emergency, patient lacks capacity, no surrogate available → implied consent; operate immediately.

why.A: Cancelling would let the patient die.
why.B: Searching for family delays life-saving surgery.
why.D: Waiting for consent in shock is unsafe.

stem: A 65-year-old patient is postoperative day 2 after abdominal surgery. He develops tachycardia, hypotension, fever, and cold extremities, with elevated lactate, Bedside point-of-care ultrasound shows a collapsed inferior vena cava (IVC) and a hyperdynamic left ventricle. Which of the following best describes the underlying pathophysiology of his condition?

opts.t: Systemic vasodilation with decreased systemic vascular resistance (SVR)

expl: Fever + hypotension with a hyperdynamic LV and collapsed IVC = distributive (septic) shock from systemic vasodilation and low SVR.

why.A: Pump failure would give a poor LV and full IVC.
why.B: Hypovolemia gives a collapsed IVC too, but fever and a hyperdynamic heart point to sepsis.

stem: A 30-year-old man presents after blunt abdominal trauma. He is hemodynamically stable but develops severe abdominal pain, guarding, and rebound tenderness. What is the most appropriate management?

opts.t: Focused assessment with sonography for trauma (FAST) only

expl: Peritonitis (guarding, rebound) after blunt trauma means hollow-viscus injury → laparotomy even in a stable patient.

why.C: Peritonitis is already an indication for surgery.

stem: A 25-year-old gentleman involved in a MVA crash as an unbelted driver. He presented to the ER with a blood pressure of 80/50 and heart rate of 70. He was unable to move his limbs below the level of elbow flexion bilaterally. He also lost sensation below the shoulder level including sphincters. What is the most important first line management?
expl: Cervical cord injury (C5–C6 level) with hypotension and relative bradycardia = neurogenic shock → IV fluids first, then vasopressors (noradrenaline, ± atropine); immobilize. Steroids aren't recommended.

why.A: Methylprednisolone isn't recommended (complications, no clear benefit).

stem: A 35-year-old male presents after a high-energy motor vehicle accident with a pelvic fracture. A pelvic binder is applied, and initial resuscitation is started. A FAST ultrasound exam shows no intra-abdominal free fluid, and no other obvious external bleeding is noted. Despite resuscitation, the patient continues to be hypotensive and shows signs of ongoing hemorrhagic shock. What is the most likely source of ongoing bleeding?

opts.t: Retroperitoneal bleeding from the pelvic fracture

expl: After a pelvic fracture with negative FAST and no other source, ongoing shock comes from retroperitoneal (pelvic) bleeding — FAST can't see the retroperitoneum.

stem: A 30-year-old male presents with a penetrating thigh injury. On examination, he has a hematoma at the site of injury, but it is not expanding, there is no active bleeding, and his distal pulses are palpable but slightly weak. He is hemodynamically stable and has no neurological deficits. What is the most appropriate next step?
expl: The source had no key ("B or C"). Soft signs only (non-expanding haematoma, slightly weak pulses) in a stable patient → CT angiography to exclude arterial injury (ABI < 0.9 also prompts imaging). Hard signs would mean surgery.

why.C: Serial exams alone are acceptable only with normal pulses/ABI.

stem: A trauma patient is hemodynamically unstable and requires immediate blood transfusion. There is no time for blood type matching. Which blood type should be given initially?
expl: Uncross-matched emergency transfusion uses group O (universal donor red cells) — O negative for women of child-bearing age (O positive acceptable in men in many protocols).

why.A: O positive is often used in men, but the universal answer is O negative.
why.C: AB is the universal plasma donor, not red cells.
why.D: Type B is incompatible with A and O.

stem: A trauma patient is undergoing primary survey according to ATLS protocol. Which of the following life-threatening conditions is primarily assessed and managed during this phase?
expl: The primary survey treats immediate threats to life — hypoxia (airway/breathing), shock, neurological deterioration. Fractures and organ injuries are found later.

why.A: Long-bone fractures are secondary-survey issues (unless bleeding massively).
why.C: Organ injuries are defined later by imaging.
why.D: Spinal fractures are protected, not defined, in the primary survey.

stem: A 28-year-old male presents after blunt abdominal trauma. He is hemodynamically stable. FAST exam is positive. What is the next best step?

opts.t: CT scan of abdomen with contrast

expl: Stable patient with a positive FAST → CT abdomen with contrast to define the injury (non-operative management is possible); unstable + positive FAST → laparotomy.

stem: A patient presents with an open book pelvic fracture. A pelvic binder is applied, but the patient continues to bleed. What is the most likely source of bleeding?
expl: Keyed venous: ~85–90% of pelvic fracture bleeding is venous (presacral plexus) and fracture surfaces — controlled by the binder and pre-peritoneal packing. Ongoing bleeding despite a binder may also be arterial (→ angioembolization).

why.A: Arterial bleeding is ~10–15% — the indication for angioembolization.
why.C: Bone bleeding contributes but isn't the main source.

stem: A patient with massive intra-abdominal bleeding underwent exploratory laparotomy and was given 6 units of packed red blood cells. Then she was found to have blood oozing from the central and peripheral lines with low platelets (33), prolonged PT,PTT,INR what do you give next?
expl: After massive transfusion, oozing from lines with prolonged PT/PTT = dilutional coagulopathy → replace clotting factors with FFP (and platelets, which are 33).

why.C: An adjunct for fibrinolysis, not the main deficit.

stem: A 65-year-old man presents with fever, altered mental status. BP was 80/50 mmHg, MAP 55. He is tachycardic (HR 120 bpm) and febrile (39.2°C). Labs show elevated creatinine (2.5 mg/dL), LDH (500 U/L), and lactate (4.5 mmol/L). What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Fever, confusion, hypotension (MAP 55), raised creatinine and lactate 4.5 = septic shock.

why.C: May be the source, but the picture is septic shock.
why.D: No bleeding described; fever points to sepsis.

stem: What is the aim of the primary survey in ATLS?
expl: The primary survey (ABCDE) aims to identify and immediately treat life-threatening injuries.

why.C: A complete neurological exam belongs to the secondary survey.

stem: A patient presents with a spleen laceration measuring 2 cm. What is the injury grade?
expl: AAST spleen: grade I laceration <1 cm deep; grade II 1–3 cm parenchymal depth not involving trabecular vessels; grade III >3 cm or involving trabecular vessels.

stem: A patient with penetrating trauma is hemodynamically stable. What is the next step in management?
expl: Haemodynamically stable penetrating trauma without peritonitis → CT with IV contrast (selective management); unstable or peritonitic → laparotomy.

why.B: Not routine in a stable patient without peritonitis.
why.C: Laparoscopy can assess peritoneal penetration in selected cases.

stem: A patient with a history of a fall presents with crescent-shaped bleeding on imaging. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Crescent-shaped (concave) extra-axial blood crossing suture lines = subdural haematoma (torn bridging veins).

stem: A patient with a lens-shaped hematoma on imaging. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: A lens-shaped (biconvex) haematoma limited by sutures = epidural haematoma (middle meningeal artery).

stem: What is the best fluid used in resuscitation for hypovolemic shock?
expl: Ringer's lactate is the preferred balanced isotonic crystalloid for hypovolemic/hemorrhagic shock (less hyperchloremic acidosis than NS).

why.A: Acceptable but large volumes cause hyperchloremic acidosis.

stem: Patient presents with stab in the anterior chest, in ER he suddenly lost pulse, what to do?
expl: Penetrating chest trauma with loss of pulse in the ER → emergency (resuscitative) thoracotomy right there — no time to move to the OR.

why.B: Moving to the OR loses the window.

stem: Female came after fight with stabbed abdomen, there was positive fluid in FAST, and signs of peritonitis, but the patient is vitally stable, what to do?
expl: Stab wound with peritonitis (and positive FAST) → laparotomy, even if stable.

why.B: CT is for stable patients without peritonitis.

stem: A child fell down and he developed just confusion. What is the diagnosis?
expl: A child with only transient confusion after a fall (no focal signs) = concussion (mild traumatic brain injury).

why.B: Acute SDH causes falling consciousness/focal signs.

stem: A 25-year-old unbelted driver has BP 80/50 and HR 70, can't move his limbs below elbow flexion, and has lost sensation below the shoulders. What type of shock is this?
ansText: Neurogenic shock — cervical cord injury interrupts sympathetic outflow → hypotension with bradycardia/normal HR and warm, vasodilated skin. Treat with fluids then vasopressors.

stem: Which of the following is a hard sign of vascular injury?
srcNote: No answer key is stated in the source.
ansText: Bruit or thrill — a hard sign (with pulsatile bleeding, expanding haematoma, absent pulses, distal ischaemia) → operative exploration.

stem: Which one of the following can’t be seen by FAST?
expl: FAST looks for free fluid in the pericardium, hepatorenal (Morison's) pouch, splenorenal recess and pelvis, and shows the solid organs around them. The pancreas is retroperitoneal and poorly seen.

why.A: The splenorenal view shows the spleen.

stem: Stab wound +vital stable +subcutaneous emphysema + increasing in size hematoma in the neck ?
expl: Penetrating neck injury with hard signs (expanding haematoma, subcutaneous emphysema = airway/aerodigestive injury) → emergency neck exploration even if stable.

why.C: CT angiography is for stable patients without hard signs.

stem: A 31 years old female in her third trimester had a motor vehicle accident. She is already on a spine board. What is the best position to communicate to the team on scene :

opts.t: Keep her supine on her back
Tilt to the right side to prevent hypotension
Tilt to the left side to prevent hypotension

expl: In late pregnancy the uterus compresses the IVC when supine → tilt the spine board to the LEFT (15–30°) or displace the uterus manually.

why.A: Head elevation doesn't relieve caval compression.

stem: Patient have stab wound in right chest , stable you do cxr you found small pneumothorax and moderate effusion what is next step?
expl: Traumatic pneumothorax with a haemothorax (moderate effusion) after a stab → chest tube (drains blood and air, monitors ongoing bleeding).

why.C: Moderate haemothorax shouldn't just be observed.

stem: A case about a female with a high speed motor vehicle accident at 100km/hr with seatbelt sign and FAST showed free fluid in the pelvic. What is the likely damaged organ :
expl: Seatbelt sign + free fluid after high-speed deceleration → hollow viscus injury, most often small bowel (and mesentery) ± Chance fracture.

stem: patient presented to the ER with a knife stab on epigastric and lost a significant amount of blood on the scene. Hemodynamically stable and was given IV fluid resuscitation and activated massive blood transfusion code. What is the next best step:
expl: Stab wound with major blood loss requiring massive transfusion → open laparotomy (bleeding source control).

why.A: Local exploration is for stable superficial wounds.
why.B: CT is for stable patients without ongoing bleeding.

stem: patient has abdominal trauma. Do you find sub-capsular hematoma less than 10% what is the grade?
expl: Splenic grade I = subcapsular haematoma < 10% surface area (laceration < 1 cm deep).

stem: Which of the following is known as a “ triad for death”?
expl: The lethal triad of trauma: acidosis, hypothermia and coagulopathy — each worsens the others; damage-control surgery aims to break it.

stem: A 35-year-old patient presented with trauma history, his blood pressure is normal, patient is stable after the CT you found that there is liver injury grade 2 what is your next step in management ?

opts.t: admit the patient and do serial cbc

expl: Stable patient with a grade II liver injury → non-operative management: admit, monitor, serial Hb/CBC.

why.A: Not needed in a stable patient.
why.D: Angioembolization is for a contrast blush/ongoing bleeding.

stem: A patient with a blunt splenic injury, CT angio showed extravasation blush. The patient was hemodynamically stable. What is the next step?

opts.t: Monitor with serial CBC and Hb

expl: A haemodynamically stable patient with a contrast blush (active arterial bleeding) on CT → angioembolisation (non-operative management). Unstable → laparotomy.

why.D: Blush = high risk of failure with observation alone.

stem: A gentleman has an MVA with multiple injuries…upon primary survey the patient was stable When FAST was done all the 4 quadrants were positive for blood, IV fluid and blood were given to the patient. What is the next step in management?
expl: Free blood in all four quadrants with ongoing need for fluids and blood = major haemorrhage → exploratory laparotomy (no CT).

stem: A patient had MVA during the primary survey you noticed rib fracture and tracheal deviation, the patient had difficulty in breathing. While auscultating there was decreased breathing sound in the right chest wall. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Rib fracture, tracheal deviation, difficulty breathing and decreased breath sounds → tension pneumothorax.

why.C: A minimal pneumothorax doesn't shift the trachea.

stem: Patient presented to the ER after trauma on examination the HR was 100 and the BP was low. GCS was 7 and he is on 10 L nasal oxygenation, what are you going to do next :
expl: GCS 7 (≤8) → secure a definitive airway (intubate).

stem: Patient MVA, was hypotensive and tachycardiac then resuscitated and get improved, with examination the pelvis was unstable and pelvic binder was applied, FAST revealed blood in the abdominal cavity. What is most appropriate next step?

opts.t: Pelvic binder is the definitive management

expl: Unstable pelvic fracture with a positive FAST (intraperitoneal bleeding) after resuscitation → laparotomy (abdominal bleeding) with pre-peritoneal pelvic packing.

why.B: Angioembolization is for stable patients/arterial bleeding without abdominal bleeding.

stem: A 36 years old patient presented with a hemothorax after a gunshot. After the initial resuscitation, he was managed by placement of a chest tube that drained 1600 cc, what is the best next step ?
expl: Massive haemothorax — > 1500 mL immediately (or > 200 mL/h for 2–4 h) → thoracotomy.

stem: A case about a trauma patient who was presented with a pelvic fracture which is managed by pelvic binders with ( + ) FAST , and asked about what is the next step ?
expl: Pelvic fracture with binder and positive FAST (abdominal bleeding) → emergency laparotomy with pelvic packing.

why.A: Angioembolization if FAST negative and arterial bleeding suspected.

stem: A child was brought to the ER after hitting the handlebar while cycling. He has abdominal pain and has not been able to eat at all. What is the most likely organ to be damaged?
expl: Handlebar injury in a child → duodenal haematoma/injury (or pancreas) — compressed against the spine; vomiting and inability to eat.

stem: A case about a female who experienced a car crash from her left side, and on PE they found that she has fractured ribs from the 7th to the 10th. And asks about what could be possibly injured in the patient ?
srcNote: (liver and splenic diseases and pancreatic masses)
expl: Left lower rib fractures (7th–10th/9th–12th) are associated with splenic injury (right-sided → liver).

stem: What is the artery injured during posterior Knee dislocation
expl: Posterior knee dislocation stretches/tears the popliteal artery (tethered at the adductor hiatus and soleus arch) → check ABI/angiography.

why.B: Deep femoral isn't at the knee.

stem: A patient had a blunt liver injury that was classified as grade 3 liver injury. The patient was stable and on CT there was extravasation of contrast. Which of the following is the best management?
expl: Stable patient with a grade III liver injury and contrast extravasation → angioembolization (non-operative). Packing is for unstable patients at laparotomy.

stem: A 20-year-old man brought to the ED 20 minutes after an MVA. On examination, he was drowsy with warm extremities. Temp: 36.5, BP:80/40 mmHg, pulse: 50 beats/min. These findings are the best explained by which of the following types of shocks?
expl: Hypotension with BRADYCARDIA and warm extremities after trauma = neurogenic shock (loss of sympathetic tone from spinal cord injury).

stem: A 29 y/o woman was involved in a motor vehicle collision with prolonged extraction from the car due to lower limbs entrapment in the front dashboard. At the emergency department, she is able to talk, C-collar in situ, chest exam shows equal air entry bilaterally with no add sounds. Her manual BP 88/56 mmHg, Pulse 121 beats /min, with no obvious external bleeding. Her GCS 14/15 What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

opts.t: Bolus of one liter IV ringer lactate
Transfusion of two units of O- blood

srcNote: (Trauma)(Principles of fluids and electrolytes balance in surgical patient)
expl: Hypotensive trauma patient talking, no airway problem → start resuscitation with a 1 L warm RL bolus (ATLS), then reassess and give blood if non-responder.

why.C: Blood comes if she doesn't respond (or in class III/IV hemorrhage).
why.D: Surgical consult is needed, but resuscitation starts now.

stem: A 33-year-old man, brought to the ER after he was involved in road traffic accident. Primary and secondary surveys revealed intra-abdominal bleeding with multiple long bone fractures. Temperature: 37.2 C BP: 85/50 mmHg, HR: 135/min Which of the following is the most appropriate method to give narcotic analgesia?
srcNote: (Miscellaneous) Source note (433 A Q42): ( Miscellaneous ) Explanation: Opioid drugs such as morphine or diamorphine, given in small intravenous doses (intramuscular absorption may be poor and inconsistent). Reference: Davidson 6th ed. ch. 7 p. 99
expl: In shock, peripheral perfusion is poor, so IM/SC absorption is unpredictable → give opioids in small IV boluses.

stem: A 32 y/o construction worker is brought to the hospital after a workplace related accident, where he fell from a height of 4 meters. He is having inspiratory stridor and has oxygen saturation of 88% on high flow oxygen via a non-rebreathing mask. Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

opts.t: Maintain 100% oxygen and obtain immediate cervical spine X-ray
Maintain inline immobilization and establish a definite airway

expl: Stridor with SpO₂ 88% on high-flow O₂ after a fall → airway is failing; keep the C-spine immobilized in line and secure a definitive airway (intubation).

why.B: Imaging must not delay the airway.

stem: A 19-year-old man with no past medical history, presents with one day of fever and persistent vomiting of blood. On examination he looks drowsy and sweaty with cold skin and pallor. His blood pressure is 90/50, heart rate is 130/minute and respiratory rate is 30/minute Which one of the following is the most appropriate initial step in the management?
expl: Drowsy, sweaty, hypotensive patient vomiting blood → ABC: ensure the airway first (aspiration risk), then circulation.

stem: A 35 y/o male presented to your emergency department after being stabbed in the chest, on inspection the patient has an isolated stab wound in the right side of the chest. His vital signs are as follows: BP: 80/40 mmHg, pulse 130/min, RR 32/min. Glasgow coma scale is 15/15. What is the most appropriate initial step in his management?
srcNote: (Trauma) Source note (435 F Q12): A stab wound presentation is most likely indicative of hemothorax which requires immediate chest tube insertion
expl: Right chest stab with shock (BP 80/40) — massive haemothorax/pneumothorax → chest tube (if signs of tension, needle first). The source: a stab wound most likely causes a haemothorax needing an immediate chest tube.

stem: A 19 y/o man sustained a motor vehicle collision, presented to the ED. He was severely agitated with bloody secretions from his mouth and was in clear respiratory distress. There was an apparent fracture of the left femur with significant blood oozing. Which of the following actions is considered top priority in this patient?

opts.t: Immediate application of pressure over the left femur.
Suctioning the mouth with a rigid suction catheter.

expl: Airway first — bloody secretions threaten the airway → suction with a rigid (Yankauer) catheter before anything else, then breathing, then control the femoral bleeding.

why.D: Oxygen through a blocked airway doesn't help.

stem: A 35-year old pedestrian hit by a motor vehicle is brought to the emergency department. On arrival, his blood pressure is 84/60, pulse rate is 128/minute, respiratory rate of 20/minute, oxygen saturation is 89%, and Glasgow coma score is 11. He has no visible external bleeding. Patient moans his pelvis is palpated. Management of his airway, and ventilation with rapid fluid resuscitation were initiated. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
srcNote: (Trauma) Source note (434 Q11): major pelvic fractures pose a difficult management problem, as conventional splintage is impossible and massive and uncontrollable blood loss may result. The optimal approach is the application of external fixator devices in the resuscitation phase, followed, if required, by angiographic embolization. If not done by prehospital providers, the pelvis should be rapidly stabilized with a sheet or commercial pelvic external stabilizer. Reference: Davidson 6th ed. ch. 7 p. 97
expl: Hypotensive pedestrian with a painful pelvis and no external bleeding → suspect pelvic haemorrhage → pelvic binder immediately (reduces volume, tamponades venous bleeding).

stem: A 38-year old man involved in a motor vehicle collision. During trauma survey a pelvic crepitus and an enlarging perineal hematoma are detected. His abdomen is rigid. FAST exam was positive. After initial resuscitation his vitals are as follows: HR: 130 , BP:70/40 , RR: 23 , TEMP.: 36.6 , SPO2: 98% in room air. Which of the following is the appropriate next step in management?

opts.t: CT of the abdomen and pelvis.
Wrapping the pelvis with a bed sheets.

expl: Pelvic crepitus + perineal haematoma + shock → first wrap the pelvis (sheet/binder) to control pelvic bleeding, then laparotomy for the positive FAST.

stem: Patient presented with sepsis, had a subclavian central line inserted. 2 hours later, he became tachycardic, his BP and O2 saturation dropped, what’s the most likely cause? (incomplete question)
srcNote: (Practical Procedures and Investigation of Surgical Patients)
expl: Hypotension, tachycardia and desaturation shortly after a subclavian line → iatrogenic tension pneumothorax.

stem: A 50 y/o man, who is known to have peptic ulcer disease is brought to the hospital with a history of vomiting bright red blood 3 times at home. On initial examination, he produced incomprehensible sounds, opened his eyes on painful stimuli and was able to localize painful stimuli. His pulse is 120 bpm, BP 85/60 mmHg. O2 saturation is 93% on room air. Which one of the following is the most appropriate 1st step in the management of this patient?
expl: GCS ~9 (E2V2M5) with hematemesis → the airway is at risk → airway control first.

stem: A 25-year-old man was brought to the ER after he was involved in a motor Vehicle accident. On Arrival, he was conscious, BP 85/55 mmHg, HR 110b/m, with tenderness in the right upper quadrant of the abdomen and chest. IV fluid resuscitation was initiated and his blood pressure became 108/66 mmHg and HR=95 b/m. Which of the following is the appropriate next step?
srcNote: (Trauma) Source note (433 A Q1): even if there is FAST, the answer won’t change “according to doctor’s notes” as the patient is stable and regardless FAST result we’ll do CT
expl: The patient responded to fluids (now stable) → CT abdomen to define injuries (the source: even with FAST, a stable patient goes to CT).

stem: A 35-year old unrestrained driver involved in a motor vehicle accident is brought to the emergency department. On arriving, he is complaining of chest pain. His blood pressure is 60/40, and pulse rate is 128/minute. He is diaphoretic, and has a respiratory rate of 40/minute. Which one of the following clinical findings best differentiates cardiac tamponade from tension pneumothorax in this patient?
expl: Both tamponade and tension pneumothorax cause shock with raised JVP; breath sounds are reduced/absent on one side only in tension pneumothorax.

stem: A gentleman was involved in a MVA, he was unrestrained driver, hemodynamically unstable, unconscious, O2 sat 81%. He was not moving any of his limbs. What is the most appropriate next step?

opts.t: Put the patient on the lateral side "recovery position".

expl: Unconscious trauma patient with possible cervical spine injury → open the airway with a jaw thrust (no head tilt).

stem: a patient presented after a trauma with splenic rupture. He had a splenectomy. A year later he presented with hypotension, fever, and septic shock. What is the most likely organism?
expl: After splenectomy, overwhelming post-splenectomy infection is caused by encapsulated organisms — mostly Streptococcus pneumoniae.

stem: A patient presented with a life-threatening vascular injury after a RTA. No watcher was there in the scene. What to do regarding his consent?

opts.t: Try to find a family member
Try to get a verbal consent from a family member

expl: Life-threatening injury and no one available → implied consent; treat immediately.

stem: Calculate MAP (mean arterial pressure) given that BP 80/50?
expl: MAP = DBP + (SBP − DBP)/3 = 50 + 10 = 60.

stem: After initial head trauma, which of the following conditions will lead to secondary brain injury?
expl: Secondary brain injury follows hypoxia and hypotension (also hypercapnia, raised ICP, hyper/hypoglycaemia, fever) — prevent them.

why.D: Hyponatraemia worsens oedema, but hypoxia is the classic answer.

stem: 52 y/o male patient was brought to emergency department unconscious after falling from a bridge about 6 meters high. His initial observations showed: T: 36.2 0C, BP: 80/50 mmHg ... What is the most accurate indicator of inadequate tissue perfusion in this patient?
expl: Lactate reflects anaerobic metabolism → the most accurate marker of inadequate tissue perfusion.

stem: Which of the following will benefit the most from ICU admission and management?

opts.t: 45 y/o female post thyroidectomy and neck dissection for cancer
24 y/o male post trauma with multiple head and trunk injuries
77 y/o female with sepsis and stage 4 pancreatic cancer
65 y/o male post uncomplicated laparoscopic cholecystectomy

expl: ICU benefits patients with reversible life-threatening conditions needing close monitoring — a young polytrauma patient with head and trunk injuries.

why.C: Palliative; ICU unlikely to change outcome.

stem: A patient presented in the ER with tension pneumothorax undergoing, which of the following is irrelevant?

opts.t: Confirm the chest tube insertion with CT
insert at the level of the nipple, midaxillary
low pressure volume can be useful sometimes

srcNote: (practical procedures and investigation of surgical patient)
expl: Chest-tube placement is confirmed with a chest X-ray, not CT. Asepsis, the 5th ICS at nipple level in the mid-axillary line, and low-pressure suction when needed are all relevant.

stem: Woman post MVA. What's the most likely diagnosis? Original source figure: 438 F Q24
expl: Contrast extravasating around the bladder base in a "molar tooth"/flame pattern confined to the pelvis = extraperitoneal bladder rupture (usually with pelvic fracture; treated with catheter drainage). Intraperitoneal rupture outlines bowel loops.

stem: A35-year-old female is brought to the emergency department by the Red Crescent after a motor vehicle collision. The patient is not opening his eye to pain, producing incomprehensible sounds and on painful stimulus he extends his arms, What is his Glasgow Coma Score (GCS)?
srcNote: (Trauma) Source note (436 A Q28): Dcerebrating 2 eye closed 1 incomprehensible sounds 2
expl: Eyes none = 1, incomprehensible sounds = 2, extension (decerebrate) = 2 → GCS 5.

stem: Ideal location for chest tube?

opts.t: 4th intercostal space above 5th rib midaxillary line

expl: Chest tube: 4th/5th intercostal space, above the rib (to spare the neurovascular bundle under the rib above), between the anterior and mid-axillary lines.

why.B: Below the rib injures the neurovascular bundle.

stem: Patient with electrical burn, and fell from 3m height, he is unconscious. entry point is right shoulder, exit point left shoulder. What is the next step?
expl: Unconscious patient (electrical injury + fall) cannot protect the airway → intubation (with C-spine protection) first; cardiac monitoring follows.

stem: Which of the following in not an indication for chest tube insertion?
expl: Chest tubes drain the pleural space (pneumothorax, haemothorax, chylothorax, empyema). Pneumoperitoneum is in the abdomen.

stem: Which of the following is correct regarding intestinal injury?

opts.t: Can be missed by CT with contrast

srcNote: is correct if more than 50% or destructive. (Trauma)
expl: Small-bowel injury is easily missed on CT (subtle signs) and by FAST; minor injuries are repaired primarily, while destructive injuries (> 50% circumference) need resection and anastomosis. The source accepted B and C.

why.A: Penetrating injury is more common for bowel.

stem: a long scenario of a patient which has been stabbed in the abdomen and he is stable with Intestinal evisceration. Which of the following is the antibiotic of choice to prevent surgical site infection?
expl: Penetrating abdominal trauma with evisceration → bowel flora prophylaxis covering gram-negatives and anaerobes: ceftriaxone + metronidazole.

stem: A Pregnant patient presented with massive bleeding, but she was stable. What is the reason behind her normal vital signs?
expl: Keyed increased heart rate. Pregnancy raises heart rate (by 10–15/min), stroke volume and blood volume, so vital signs stay normal despite significant bleeding.

stem: Regarding trauma and splenic laceration. Which of the following is contraindicated in non-operative management?
srcNote: (Trauma) explanation: in a small center either you do splenectomy or Transfer to a big center.
expl: Non-operative management of splenic injury needs ICU monitoring, IR, blood bank and a surgeon available 24 h. In a peripheral hospital without these, operate or transfer. High grade alone isn't an absolute contraindication if stable.

why.A: High grade isn't an absolute contraindication when stable.

stem: Grade 4 spleen injury, after resuscitation she became stable, CT shows grade 4 splenic injury and extravasation. What's the next step in management?
expl: Grade IV splenic injury with extravasation in a patient now stable → non-operative management with angioembolization (if resources exist); unstable → splenectomy.

why.D: Splenorrhaphy is for selected lower grades at laparotomy.

stem: 21 y/o man brought to the emergency department with history of motorbike crash. He was conscious, oriented with O2 saturation of 85% on room air and hypertympanic percussion on left hemi-thorax. Temperature: 36.7 0C, BP: 80/40 mmHg, Pulse: 140 beat/min Which of the following is most likely diagnosis?
expl: Hypoxia, hypotension, tachycardia and a hyper-tympanic hemithorax after trauma = tension pneumothorax.

stem: 32-year-old patient is a victim of an assault. Upon presentation he is found to be in a stable condition. His workup revealed a grade 4 liver laceration with no active bleeding, a small subdural hematoma with no signs of raised intracranial pressure What is the main advantage of admitting this patient to ICU?
expl: A stable patient with a high-grade liver injury and an SDH can deteriorate — ICU allows close hemodynamic and neurological monitoring.

stem: Which of the following most likely to be injured through penetrating trauma?
expl: The right ventricle forms most of the anterior surface of the heart, so it is most often injured in penetrating chest trauma.

stem: Which one of the following is mostly missed in primary survey?
expl: Blunt cardiac contusion is subtle (arrhythmias, ECG changes) and easily missed in the primary survey; open pneumothorax and massive haemothorax are obvious.

why.D: A large extradural haematoma causes obvious neurological signs.

stem: A 30 years old male had an RTA and was hemodynamically unstable, imaging showed 4 cm laceration in spleen and he was taken to OR . What is the best management?
expl: Unstable patient with a large splenic laceration taken to theatre → complete (total) splenectomy (fastest and safest); splenorrhaphy/partial splenectomy only in stable selected cases.

stem: An 18 years old woman developed urticaria and wheezing following IV injection contrast for abdominal CT scan. Her Bp is 120/80 , pulse 120/minute and respiratory rate was 30/min. Which ONE of the following is the appropriate immediate therapy?
srcNote: Source note (436 A Q23): The question was cancelled because more than 50% answered wrong. The course organizer told us the answer is Epinephrine. Source note (429 F Q19): anaphylaxic shock
expl: Urticaria + wheeze after contrast = anaphylaxis → epinephrine (IM). The question was cancelled because many answered wrong; the organizer confirmed epinephrine.

stem: Which of the following is a site of insertion for needle decompression for tension pneumothorax?
expl: Classic needle decompression: 2nd intercostal space, mid-clavicular line (ATLS 10th ed. prefers the 4th/5th ICS mid-axillary line in adults because the chest wall is thinner there).

why.C: Mid-axillary (not mid-clavicular) for the lateral approach.

stem: Which of the following is the most common site for venous cutdown to use in resuscitation of a 28 year-old male in hypovolemic shock due to abdominal blunt trauma?
expl: Venous cut-down: great saphenous vein anterior to the medial malleolus.

why.D: Small saphenous runs behind the lateral malleolus — not the standard.

stem: When inserting a chest tube which one of the following is done?

opts.t: A tube size of 12-14 Fr is commonly used for adults

expl: Chest-tube insertion is a sterile procedure under local anaesthesia; adult trauma tubes are large (28–32 Fr for haemothorax); CT isn't needed.

stem: A patient was brought to the ER after a fall from height, he had subdural hematoma and other injuries. He was admitted to ICU, what's the most likely reason?

opts.t: To facilitate the discussion between patient and family

expl: Patients with SDH and other injuries go to ICU for advanced hemodynamic and neurological monitoring.

stem: Patient after RTA, admitted in hospital was unstable, exam found hemoperitoneum and found to have 3.5 cm hematoma on spleen. Was taken to OR and a laparotomy was done. What is the best management?
expl: An unstable patient with haemoperitoneum from a splenic injury taken to laparotomy → total splenectomy (fast, definitive). Splenic preservation is for stable patients/children.

stem: A 45-year-old man presented to the hospital with acute left leg ischemia secondary to trauma After revascularization, the patient should be observed for potential complication. Which complication is most likely to occur secondary to reperfusion syndrome?
expl: Reperfusion of an ischaemic limb washes potassium, lactic acid and myoglobin from dead muscle into the circulation → hyperkalaemia (arrhythmias), metabolic acidosis, myoglobinuric renal failure, plus compartment syndrome. (The source writes "Ans. A".)

stem: a 7-year-old boy sustained a straddle injury while jumping with his bike. He had urethral bleeding and difficulty in voiding. What is the next step in managing this patient?

opts.t: Stop the bleeding by penile compression
Insert urethral foley catheter to relief his urine retention

srcNote: Source key was B; corrected — see explanation. (Investigation of Urinary tract Problems & Renal Colic)
expl: Straddle injury + blood at the meatus + difficulty voiding = urethral injury (bulbar) → retrograde (ascending) urethrogram first; never blind catheterization (suprapubic catheter if retention). The source keyed penile compression, which isn't the management.

why.A: Exploration is for complete rupture after imaging.
why.D: Catheterization can convert a partial tear into a complete one.

stem: Young man presented to ER with right leg cellulitis. Upon starting IV Penicillin G he had shortness of breath and BP became lower and pulse 43 bpm. What is the initial step?
expl: Anaphylaxis to penicillin: the first step is to stop the offending drug, then airway, adrenaline and fluids.

why.B: Next (after stopping the trigger) if the airway is compromised.
why.C: Part of treatment after stopping the drug.

stem: a 25 y/o male came to the ED presenting with a picture of right sided pneumothorax. The plan is to insert a chest tube. Which of the following would aid you in locating the site quickly? (Incomplete Q)
srcNote: , (Chest trauma) the Q was about the location of the tube (5th intercostal in the mid-to-anterior axillary line= nipple in males, inframammary line in females)
expl: The 5th intercostal space at the mid/anterior axillary line corresponds to the nipple level in men (inframammary fold in women).

stem: A labourer is brought to the emergency department unconscious after falling from a bridge about 6 meters’ height. The patient received 2 liters of bolus crystalloid intravenous fluid. His initial vitals are: BP:100/40, HR: 110/min, RR 22/min, T: 36.2 C Which of the following is the most accurate indicator of adequacy of fluid replacement?
srcNote: (Principles of Fluids and Electrolytes Balance in Surgical Patients)
expl: Urine output (≥0.5 ml/kg/h adult) is the best bedside indicator of adequate resuscitation/end-organ perfusion.

why.A: Lactate shows perfusion but lags behind.

stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: The image shows a crescent-shaped extra-axial collection → subdural haematoma.

stem: A 38-year-old man was brought to the ER after he was involved in MVA, on arrival, he was agitated, BP=90/56 mmHg, HR=107b/m, tenderness with reduced air entry over the right side of the chest and normal abdominal examination. The arterial ABG result are listed below: pH = 7.3 HCO3 = 18 PaCO2 = 52 SaO2= 80 Which of the following is the appropriate next step?
srcNote: (Trauma) in case of respiratory distress secondary to pneumothorax, breathing takes priority over airway in the initial trauma survey. - Uptodate Source note (433 A Q2): unstable patients with traumatic pneumothorax: needle thoracostomy (failed?) > finger thoracostomy > (consider chest tube for bilateral pneumothorax , patient requires mechanical ventilation or doesn’t meet pneumothorax stability criteria) - AMBOSS
expl: Trauma, agitation, hypotension, reduced air entry and tenderness on one side with respiratory acidosis and low saturation = tension pneumothorax → immediate needle decompression (breathing problem threatening life; don't wait for X-ray). Source note: unstable traumatic pneumothorax → needle (or finger) thoracostomy, then chest tube.

why.A: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis — no X-ray first.
why.B: Definitive, but decompression comes first in the unstable patient.
why.C: Intubation with positive pressure worsens a tension pneumothorax.

stem: In patients with raised ICP secondary to severe traumatic brain injury, hyperventilation may be considered as a temporary procedure to reduce the ICP. When using this modality profound hypocarbia must be avoided to prevent which of the following?

opts.t: Shift of oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve to left.
Respiratory acidosis leading to secondary cerebral edema.

srcNote: , (Principles of Fluids and Electrolytes Balance in Surgical Patients) Davidson P:458
expl: Hypocarbia causes cerebral vasoconstriction → ICP falls but cerebral ischemia follows if PCO₂ drops too far.

why.C: True but not the main danger.

stem: A 31-year old man, construction worker fell from 3 meters height at workplace, brought to emergency department shocked with BP 80/50 mmHg and pulse 130/minute. No obvious external bleeding. Which of the following is the initial fluid of choice for resuscitation?
srcNote: (Principles of Fluids and Electrolytes Balance in Surgical Patients)
expl: Shocked trauma patient → isotonic crystalloid (RL) first, then blood if no response.

why.A: Blood comes after the initial bolus (or immediately in class III–IV).

stem: A 15 years old male involved in MVA brought to the ED and upon your investigation you concluded that the patient has tension pneumothorax and hypotension. What type of shock does this patient have ?
expl: Tension pneumothorax → obstructive shock.

stem: A 38 year old man involved in a motor vehicle collision. During his trauma survey pelvic crepitus and an enlarging perineal hematoma are detected. His abdomen is soft and lax, FAST exam was positive. After initial resuscitation, his vital are as follows: HR: 130 beat/min BP: 70/40 mmHg RR: 23/min Temp: 36.6 C SPO2: 98% on room air What is the best next step in management

opts.t: CT of the abdomen and pelvis
Wrapping the pelvis with a bed sheet

expl: Unstable pelvic fracture → immediate pelvic wrapping/binder as part of circulation control.

why.A: Laparotomy after pelvic stabilization if FAST positive and unstable.

stem: 32 y\o man brought to the ER after involvement in a RTA. On examination he was dyspneic with severe maxillofacial injury. Which of the following urgent airway control method is appropriate?
expl: Severe maxillofacial injury with dyspnoea → oral/nasal intubation may be impossible or dangerous → surgical airway (cricothyroidotomy).

why.C: Often impossible with severe facial trauma.

stem: How many areas are assessed with FAST?
expl: FAST = 4 views: pericardial (subxiphoid), RUQ (hepatorenal), LUQ (splenorenal), pelvis. eFAST adds both hemithoraces.

stem: Which of the following is the leading cause of death and disability in trauma patients?
expl: Head injury is the leading cause of trauma death and disability.

stem: 53 y/o woman admitted to intensive care unit with severe pancreatitis complicated by sepsis. On examination she was having generalized edema with hypotension in spite of large amount of intravenous Ringer's lactate infusion. Which of the following is the most likely body fluid abnormality this patient may have?
expl: Capillary leak in severe pancreatitis/sepsis → third-space losses: edema with intravascular depletion (hypotension) despite fluids.

stem: A 32 y\o man brought to ER with history of stab wound in the right thigh. On examination he was unconscious, and pale with active bleeding from the wound. Temperature: 36.7 Blood pressure: 70\40 mmHg. Pulse: 140 beat\min. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in management?
srcNote: Source note (429 F Q2): Ppt stage 4 hypovolemic shock > he bleed till he lost his conscious
expl: Unconscious patient in class IV shock (BP 70/40, HR 140) → secure the airway first (ABC), while controlling bleeding and resuscitating in parallel.

why.A: Done simultaneously, but the airway comes first in the sequence.

stem: A 30 year old football player sustained head trauma and is unresponsive and snoring loudly. What is the best way to open his airway?

opts.t: Put the patient on his side

expl: Snoring = tongue obstructing the airway in an unconscious head-injured patient → jaw thrust (protects the C-spine).

stem: A 25 year old man is brought to the hospital after a gunshot wound to the right arm approximately 15 minutes prior to arrival. Which of the following findings on a physical exam suggest the presence of an arterial injury requiring urgent angiography or surgical intervention?

opts.t: Proximity of the injury to major vascular structure

srcNote: Source note (431 A Q25): ( Trauma ) (according to lawrence page 209) diminished pulses are considered soft signs which suggest vascular injury
expl: Keyed diminished distal pulses — a sign of arterial injury needing angiography/intervention (soft sign per Lawrence; hard if absent). Hypotension, nerve injury and proximity are non-specific.

why.D: Proximity alone is a weak soft sign.

stem: A 25 y\o patient came to ED with a history of diffuse abdominal pain for 4 days. Physical examination revealed diffuse abdominal distention and tenderness with sluggish bowel sounds. Laboratory values showed: WBC 21*109/l, with normal amylase. He underwent exploratory laparotomy and found to have perforated duodenal ulcer with diffuse peritoneal soiling with purulent material. Temperature: 39. Blood pressure: 85\50 mmHg. Pulse: 125 beat\min Which of the following characterize the shock state of this patient?
srcNote: Source note (429 F Q1): septic shock, Infection triggers a cytokine-mediated proinflammatory response that results in peripheral vasodilation, redistribution of blood flow, endothelial cell activation, increased vascular permeability and the formation of microthrombi within the microcirculation. Cardiac output typically increases in septic shock to compensate for the peripheral vasodilation. However, despite a global increase in oxygen delivery, microcirculatory dysfunction impairs oxygen delivery to the cells. Compounding disturbances in oxygen delivery, mitochondrial dysfunction blocks the normal bioenergetic pathways within the cell impairing oxygen utilization. Davidson page number 18, chapter one
expl: Septic shock from purulent peritonitis: cytokines cause peripheral vasodilation, with compensatory high cardiac output.

why.C: Also seen in early sepsis, but the keyed defining feature is vasodilation.

stem: Patient with fever and tachycardia with normal BP but high WBC in urine and high urea and creatinine , MAP= 75 .. what is it ?
srcNote: ( because there is organ damage ) Source figure: 432 F Q61
expl: Old terminology: SIRS + infection = sepsis; sepsis + organ dysfunction (raised urea/creatinine) = severe sepsis; with hypotension unresponsive to fluids = septic shock. MAP 75 is not shock.

why.A: There is infection and organ dysfunction.

stem: 68 year old female had hypovolemic shock due to splenic rupture and underwent splenectomy, and was transfused 8 packed RBCs. 3 days post op she started to have fever (38.2) blood culture showed gram negative bacilli what is the most likely cause of her bacteraemia?
srcNote: Source note (432 F Q4): “As described above, the redistribution of cardiac output observed in shock leads to a marked reduction in splanchnic blood flow. In the stomach, the resulting mucosal hypoperfusion and hypoxia predispose to stress ulceration and haemorrhage. In the intestine, movement (translocation) of bacteria and/or bacterial endotoxin from the lumen to the portal vein and then systemic circulation is thought to be a key mechanism underlying the development of SIRS and multiple organ failure” -Davidsons page 22
expl: Shock reduces splanchnic perfusion → gut mucosal ischemia → bacteria/endotoxin translocate into the portal and systemic circulation → gram-negative bacteremia.

why.B: Possible but not the keyed mechanism.

stem: Which of the following is a cause of high anion gap metabolic acidosis?
srcNote: , shock causes lactic acidosis Source note (431 A Q16): ( Principles of fluids and electrolytes balance in surgical patient ) (severe hemorrhage leading to hypovolemic shock � lactic acidosis)
expl: Hemorrhagic shock → tissue hypoperfusion → lactic acidosis (high anion gap). Diarrhea and fistulas give normal-AG acidosis.

stem: What is the most rapid way to gain access in an adult trauma with difficult peripheral intravenous access?
srcNote: (Trauma) Central venous cannulation is difficult and potentially hazardous in shocked hypovolemic patients, so if percutaneous access cannot be obtained, a surgical cut-down at the saphenofemoral junction is preferable, although more time-consuming. Intraosseous access to long bones in the adult is a viable alternative for initial resuscitation.Reference: Davidson 6th ed. ch. 7 p. 98
expl: When peripheral access fails in a shocked adult, intraosseous access is the fastest alternative (cut-down and central lines take longer).

stem: Which of the following decreases the mortality of patients?
expl: Tranexamic acid (antifibrinolytic) within 3 h reduces mortality in bleeding trauma patients (CRASH-2).

why.C: rFVIIa has no proven mortality benefit.

stem: Which of the following constitutes Cushing’s triad?

opts.t: High systolic, low HR, low RR
Low systolic, high HR, low RR
High systolic, low HR, high RR
Low systolic, low HR, low RR

srcNote: physiological nervous system response to acute elevations of intracranial pressure (ICP), resulting in the Cushing triad of widened pulse pressure (increasing systolic, decreasing diastolic) bradycardia, and irregular respirations.
expl: Cushing's triad of raised ICP: hypertension (wide pulse pressure), bradycardia and irregular/slow respiration.

stem: A 20 year old male sustained a road traffic accident. He presented to the ED unconscious with warm extremities. His vitals were: BP: 80/40 mmHg PR: 120 bpm RR: 23, Temp: 36.6. Which type of shock best explains his symptoms?

opts.t: Septic Answer is: C? This Q is probably wrong since In neurogenic shock there is also bradycardia not tachycardia as in this case. “Neurogenic shock… With patients typically presenting with hypotension, bradycardia and warm, dry peripheries.” -Davidson page 20

expl: The intended answer was neurogenic shock (warm extremities after trauma), but the compilers point out that neurogenic shock gives BRADYCARDIA, not HR 120 — the question is probably flawed. With tachycardia and warm skin early after trauma, hypovolemia must still be excluded.

why.A: Usually cold extremities, but must be excluded.

stem: A 30 year old male presents to the emergency department after sustaining a motor vehicle accident and he was ejected from the vehicle. On examination the patient has a positive Battle sign Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis ?
expl: Battle's sign (mastoid bruising) = fracture of the middle cranial fossa (basal skull fracture), with raccoon eyes, CSF otorrhoea/rhinorrhoea.

stem: calculate the CCP ( CCP = MAP - ICP )
srcNote: ? treatment protocol aims to CPP equal or more than 70, so what to do to treat the low CPP immediately ? we increase MAP in hypovolemic and trauma patients by giving fluids: 2 large bore cannula Fast infusion of 2 L saline. If no fluids ? Vasoconstriction by inotropes (adrenaline, nor-adrenaline, dopamine..) CPP less than 60 = ischemia (reversible) , CPP less than 30 = infarction (irreversible) To learn how to calculate CPP check this link https://www.registerednursern.com/calculate-cpp-cerebral-perfusion-pressure-nursing/
expl: CPP = MAP − ICP. With the values given in the recall the result is 60 mmHg.

stem: A 30-year-old football player sustained maxillofacial fracture. What is the best way to open his airway?

opts.t: Put the patient on his side

expl: With facial/head trauma, assume a C-spine injury: open the airway with a jaw thrust (no head tilt).

why.D: Recovery position doesn't secure the airway in trauma.

stem: A 72 y\o man presented to ER complaining of left side chest pain radiating to the left arm since 8 hours. Physical examination was unremarkable. Investigations revealed high troponin level with ECG changes suggestive of anterior MI. Temperature: 36.5 Blood pressure: 80\50 mmHg Pulse: 115 beat\min. Which of the following is characteristic of this condition?
srcNote: ( Miscellaneous ) Source note (429 F Q4): pt in cardiogenic shock
expl: Cardiogenic shock (anterior MI): the problem is pump failure — intravascular volume is normal, CVP is high, peripheries are vasoconstricted, HR is fast.

stem: A 29 y/o man brought to the emergency department after he involved in motor vehicle accident. On examination he was drowsy with right hemo-pneumothorax and fractures of right femur and tibia. Hemodynamic resuscitation with right thoracotomy tube was done. Which of the following is most appropriate to monitor adequate volume resuscitation?
srcNote: ( Trauma) Source note (429 F Q6): After 24 h it’ll be lactate most appropriate to monitor
expl: Urine output is the standard monitor of adequate volume resuscitation.

stem: A 28 y\o man, brought to ER after involved motor vehicle accidents. On examination he was conscious. With tender and distended abdomen. Ultrasound revealed massive intra-abdominal fluids. Temperature 36 Blood pressure 85\50mmHg Pulse 125 beat\min. Which of the following is preferred in resuscitation of this patient?
srcNote: (Trauma) (Principles of fluids and electrolytes balance in surgical patient) Source note (429 F Q10): RL is the trauma resuscitation fluid of choice because it is isotonic and it contains lactate which helps in buffering the hypovolemia-induced metabolic acidosis.
expl: Hemorrhagic shock → warm RL as the initial crystalloid, then blood.

stem: 25 y\o man, involved in RTA and underwent exploratory laparotomy. Splenectomy and repair of liver laceration. During surgery he received 12 units of pack red blood cell. Which of the following is the possible side effect of blood transfusion in this patient?
srcNote: ( Miscellaneous ) Source note (430 A Q68): ( Miscellaneous ) hypothermia, dilutional coagulopathy, hypocalcemia/hypomagnesemia & citrate toxicity, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis Source note (429 F Q20): massive blood transfusion complication. Refer to table: https://emedicine.medscape.com/article/780074-overview#a5
expl: Stored blood contains citrate anticoagulant; massive transfusion → citrate toxicity (binds calcium → hypocalcemia).

stem: Which of the following should be ruled out on primary survey?
expl: The primary survey must identify immediately life-threatening chest injuries: airway obstruction, tension pneumothorax, open pneumothorax, massive haemothorax, flail chest, tamponade. Contusion, aortic disruption and diaphragm rupture are secondary-survey findings.

stem: A 15 y/o woman Underwent appendectomy for acute appendicitis. One hour later collapsed in the recovery room. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause?
srcNote: (Surgical complications) Source note (429 F Q22): due to bleeding.
expl: Collapse within an hour of surgery is most often due to bleeding (hypovolemic shock).

stem: A 29 year old male is brought to the emergency department by the Red Crescent. On examination, patient is opening his eye to pain, producing incomprehensive sounds and to painful stimulus he flexes his arms. What is his Glasgow Coma Score?
expl: Eyes to pain = 2, incomprehensible sounds = 2, flexion (abnormal) = 3 → GCS 7.

stem: A 55 y/o woman underwent abdominal computed tomography for investigation of acute diffuse abdominal pain. During the procedure she devolved difficulty in breathing with pulse rate of 45/min and blood pressure of 90/55 mmHg. Which of the following characterize this condition?
expl: Contrast anaphylaxis → mediator-induced vasodilation and capillary leak → redistribution of intravascular volume (relative hypovolemia).

stem: A 41 y/o man admitted through emergency department complaining of right upper quadrant abdominal pain with yellowish discoloration of sclera, dark urine and fever for 5 days. On examination he was jaundiced with pulse rate of 122/min and blood pressure of 85/45 mmHg. Laboratory values showed high liver function test with dilated biliary tree in the ultrasound. Diagnosis of acute toxic cholangitis was made. Which one of the following characterizes the condition of this patient?
expl: Toxic (suppurative) cholangitis with shock = septic shock; at the cell level there is microcirculatory dysfunction impairing oxygen delivery.

stem: A 29 y/o man admitted to intensive care unit with massive upper gastrointestinal bleeding due to duodenal ulcer. While he is receiving blood transfusion, he developed fever, chest tightness and hypotension. His urine was dark in color. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Fever, chest tightness, hypotension and dark urine (hemoglobinuria) during transfusion = acute hemolytic transfusion reaction.

why.A: Doesn't explain dark urine during transfusion.

stem: A 32 y/o man victim of motor vehicle accident with massive intra-abdominal bleeding. Received 10 units of packed red blood cells within 12 hours. Which of the following is the most common complication this patient may have?
srcNote: (Principles of fluids and electrolytes balance in surgical patient)
expl: Stored blood leaks K⁺ from lysed cells → hyperkalemia after massive transfusion (also citrate toxicity/hypocalcemia, hypothermia, coagulopathy).

why.B: Acidosis early (alkalosis later from citrate metabolism).

stem: A massive blood transfusion is:

opts.t: Transfusion of half blood volume in <12 hr
Transfusion of one blood volume in 24 hr period

expl: Massive transfusion = replacing one blood volume (~10 units) in 24 h (or > 4 units in 1 h / 50% in 3 h).

stem: An 18 year old man who was involved in in a motor vehicle collision brought by paramedics to the emergency department. On examination he was conscious, GCS 13/15.and there was blood on his clothes. Patient was put on monitored bed, back board and oxygen mask. His vitals were as follow: HR: 140 beat/min BP: 75/45 mmHg RR: 28/min Oxygen saturation 98% on 100% oxygen by face mask What is the next step in management?
expl: Airway and breathing are fine (talking, SpO₂ 98%); he is in shock → next: 2 large-bore IV lines with bloods and fluid/blood resuscitation.

stem: An 8 year old boy was brought by his parents with shortness of breath after felt a sting in his neck. On examination he was drooling. Chest examination reveals reduced breath sounds and wheezing. BP: 80/50mmHg HR: 140/min RR: 30/min Temp: 37 C SpO2: 80 on face mask Which of the following is the best next step in his management?

opts.t: Salbutamol 5 mg nebulized with big flow

expl: Sting with drooling, wheeze and hypotension = anaphylaxis → IM epinephrine 0.01 mg/kg of 1:1000 is first-line.

stem: A 68 year old female was brought to the emergency department by her sister with mental status change. According to her sister the patient fell in the shower 4 days ago. Over the last 24 hours she has become less responsive and her sister was unable to wake her this afternoon. Her past medical history is significant for atrial fibrillation for which she takes warfarin. She is a recovering alcoholic and according to her sister has not had a drink in the last 5 years. On examination she has large contusion over her occiput. What is the most likely cause for her change in mental status? *
expl: An elderly patient who fell days ago and has gradually declining consciousness → chronic/subacute subdural haematoma (brain atrophy stretches bridging veins).

why.B: Epidural is acute, after a lucid interval of hours.

stem: In which of the following patients would performance of diagnostic peritoneal lavage is considered an absolute contraindication?

opts.t: Pregnant with hypotension after a blunt trauma
Expanding abdomen after a chest stab wound
Hypotension after car accident with previous abdominal surgery

srcNote: (Acute abdomen) (according to different sources, the only absolute contraindication to diagnostic peritoneal lavage is presence of the need to do exploratory laparotomy)
expl: The only absolute contraindication to DPL is an existing indication for laparotomy — an expanding abdomen after a stab wound needs the OR. Pregnancy and previous surgery are relative contraindications.

stem: A 25 year old man involved in a Motor Vehicle accident, complaining of shortness of breath. On examination. He is conscious and alert. He has reduced breath sounds on the right side and his abdomen is soft and lax. BP: 80/50 mmHg HR: 120/min RR: 32/min Temp: 37 C SpO2: 90% on face mask What is the best next step?
srcNote: (Trauma) (textbook answer, presence of hypotension makes it tension pneumothorax and requires urgent needle decompression)
expl: Reduced breath sounds + hypotension + tachypnoea after trauma = tension pneumothorax → needle decompression (source: textbook answer).

stem: A 45 year old male patient, known case liver cirrhosis and esophageal varices is brought to the hospital with history of vomiting bright red blood three times at home. On initial examination you noticed blood staining over his lips and teeth. He produces incomprehensible sounds, opens his eyes to painful stimuli and is able to localize pain. Vital sign are: Heart rate 120/min, BP: 85/60 mmHg, O2 saturation 93% on room air. After managing the airway, which one of the following is the most appropriate next step?

opts.t: Control of bleeding using sangstaken-Blakemore tube

expl: After securing the airway (GCS low), the hypotensive variceal bleeder needs immediate fluid resuscitation before endoscopy or balloon tamponade.

why.A: Bridge if bleeding can't be controlled endoscopically.

stem: A 32 year old man brought to the emergency department after he was involved in motor vehicle accident. On examination, he was drowsy and pale with tender and distended abdomen. Systemic examination, his BP was 80/45 mmHg and pulse 120/min. Which one of the following will determine the signs and symptoms of shock state in this patient?

opts.t: The amount of intravascular volume loss

srcNote: (Principles of Fluids and Electrolytes Balance in Surgical Patients)
expl: The clinical picture of hemorrhagic shock (classes I–IV) depends on how much intravascular volume has been lost.

why.A: Modifies the response but isn't the determinant.
why.D: Affects the course, not the presenting signs.

stem: Which one of the following can’t be seen by E-FAST?
expl: eFAST sees the pericardium, intraperitoneal fluid and pneumothorax/haemothorax, but not the retroperitoneum.

stem: Which one of the following formulas stand for CPP?
expl: CPP = MAP − ICP.

stem: A scenario about an open chest wound. What is your next step?
srcNote: ( Trauma) (open chest wound can cause open pneumothorax which requires a 3-sided dressing prior to giving oxygen and prior to placing a chest tube)
expl: An open (sucking) chest wound → three-sided occlusive dressing (acts as a flutter valve), then a chest tube away from the wound.

why.C: A four-sided seal can create a tension pneumothorax.

stem: Scenario about a patient with GCS 6. What is your next step?
expl: GCS ≤8 = unable to protect the airway → intubate.

why.D: Part of breathing, after the airway is secured.

stem: A scenario with a similar image. What is the diagnosis?
srcNote: ( Trauma) (Epidural hematoma has a characteristic biconvex or lentiform shape on imaging)
expl: The image shows a biconvex (lens-shaped) haematoma → epidural.

stem: Which of the following best describes the Glasgow Coma Scale Score?

opts.t: Best eye opening, orientation and motor responses.
Best eye opening, motor and sensory response.
Best eye opening, verbal and motor responses.
It has a score range between 0-15.

expl: GCS = best eye opening (4) + verbal response (5) + motor response (6); range 3–15.

stem: A 30 y/o man has been brought to the emergency department after motor vehicle accident. On examination he was conscious but he had left sided chest pain with open penetrating chest wound and labored breathing. His vitals are: BP: 100/70 mmHg, Pulse: 115/min, respiratory rate: 22/min. What is the most appropriate initial step in his management?
expl: Open chest wound with laboured breathing but stable BP → occlusive (three-sided) dressing and a chest tube (thoracostomy) through a separate incision.

stem: The picture below belongs to a patient who had sustained traumatic head injury and decreased level of consciousness.What is the sign in the below picture?
expl: Periorbital ecchymosis (raccoon eyes) = anterior cranial fossa basal skull fracture.

stem: A 17 y/o male was involved in a road traffic accident, brought to the emergency department with closed head injury and multiple other injuries. During resuscitation in the emergency room he received 2 litters of crystalloids and 3 units of packed red blood cells. After he was stabilized he moved to the ICU. His electrolytes showed Na: 135 mmol/l, Cl: 115 mmol/l and HCO3 13 (Low). What is the most appropriate fluid resuscitation at this stage?
srcNote: ( Principles of fluids and electrolytes balance in surgical patient )
expl: After 2 L of NS-type crystalloid he has hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis (Cl 115, HCO₃ 13). Further resuscitation should use a balanced solution (Ringer's lactate), not more saline.

stem: Which of the following is the most important determinant in reducing an injury when an impact occurs in a road traffic accident?
expl: Kinetic energy = ½mv² — speed matters most, so speed limitation reduces injury the most.

why.D: Mass matters less than speed squared.

stem: A 27 y/o male, involved in a road traffic accident, brought to emergency department. His vitals are: BP: 120/60 mmHg, Pulse: 100/min, RR: 22/min, O2 Sat: 95% on room air, temperature 36 0C. GCS 13/15. Which of the following should be included in your primary assessment?

opts.t: Airway, c-spine precautions, breathing and circulation.

expl: ATLS primary survey: Airway with C-spine protection → Breathing → Circulation → Disability → Exposure.

stem: A 70 y/o male patient, 6 days post-elective surgery, was brought to the emergency department with decreased level of consciousness. On examination he appears flushed and his extremities are (something ... Couldn’t remember) touch. His pulse 120/min, BP: 70/45 and oxygen saturation is 96% on 4L O2. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Flushed warm skin, hypotension, tachycardia and altered consciousness after surgery → septic (distributive) shock (compilers "not sure").

why.B: Cardiogenic shock gives cold, clammy extremities.

stem: A 20 y/o man was involved in a road traffic accident and found to be in a respiratory distress. Brought to the emergency department and he was intubated on bag valve mask. The anesthetic told you he has to use a lot of force ventilate the patient. On auscultation there is a reduced air entry on left side of the chest, trachea is deviated to the right.What is the most appropriate management option for this patient?

opts.t: Thoracostomy tube in the right 2nd intercostal space.
Thoracostomy tube in the left 2nd intercostal space.
Needle decompression on the left 2nd intercostal space.
Needle decompression on the right 2nd intercostal space.

expl: Hard to ventilate, reduced air entry on the LEFT and trachea deviated to the RIGHT → left tension pneumothorax → needle decompression on the left (2nd ICS MCL, or 4th–5th ICS in newer ATLS).

why.A: Wrong side, and a chest tube isn't the first step.

stem: A 30 y/o man is admitted to surgery department for huge abscess drainage. He was started on antibiotics and analgesics, but complains of sudden severe shortness of breath. There is no chest pain, but he is cyanosed and there was diffuse wheezing over the chest. His BP: 70/30 mmHg and HR is … tachycardic ? couldn’t remember. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
srcNote: ? Mostly because after the administration of antibiotics he developed these symptoms
expl: Sudden dyspnea, diffuse wheeze, cyanosis and hypotension right after starting antibiotics = anaphylaxis.

stem: A 30 y/o male, who is known to have diabetes and hypertension. One day after surgery started to have chest pain and sweeting. His BP: is 80/50 mmHg and pulse is 110/min. What is the most likely diagnosis?
srcNote: (Surgical Complications) because of the chest pain
expl: Chest pain, sweating and hypotension in a diabetic/hypertensive patient post-op → MI with cardiogenic shock.

stem: An 81 y/o male, who is known to have chronic liver disease, presents vomiting of blood twice at home. Upon arrival in the emergency department his BP: 85/45 mmHg, pulse: 50/min RR: 22/min. Which of the following is the initial step in management of this patient?
srcNote: ( Principles of Fluids and Electrolytes Balance in Surgical Patients ) definitive is upper gi endoscopy and we do ligation but initial we have to stabilize and give crystalloids
expl: Hypotensive variceal bleed → initial step is crystalloid resuscitation; endoscopy is definitive afterwards.

stem: A 30 y/o male, presented to the emergency department after fall from a height, he complains of severe pain at the back. On examination his BP is 85/45 mmHg, pulse is 50/min, RR is 18/min. There is a tenderness over the thoracic spines. He is unable to move both of his lower limbs with absent sensations. The rest of examination was normal. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his shock?
expl: Hypotension with bradycardia, thoracic spine tenderness and paraplegia → neurogenic shock.

stem: A 30 y/o male was involved in a road traffic accident. Upon arrival to the hospital he complained of severe pain at left thigh and his BP is 100/60, pulse is 110/min, RR is 24/min. There is a deformity at the left thigh and rest of his physical examination was normal. From the initial observations, he is in which class of hypovolemic shock?
expl: ATLS class II: 15–30% blood loss, HR 100–120, normal SBP, RR 20–30, anxious. BP 100/60 with HR 110 and RR 24 → class II.

stem: A 40 y/o lady presents to the emergency department with history of vomiting large amount of blood. The patient is known case of hepatitis C virus with liver cirrhosis. Her vitals on arrival are: BP: 90/60 mmHg, Pulse 110/min, RR 18/min and oxygen saturation is 99% on room air. Which of the following is the appropriate next step in the therapy?
expl: Hypotensive tachycardic variceal bleeder → resuscitate first.

why.C: Given early too, but resuscitation is the first step.

stem: 25 y\o man was involved in a fight. He was brought to ER with bilateral raccoon eyes and nasal bleeding. What is the immediate risk for the patient's life?
srcNote: (Trauma), Raccoon eyes = sign of basal skull fracture Source note (428 Q2): (aspiration of blood)
expl: Raccoon eyes with nasal bleeding = basal skull/midface injury → blood in the airway → airway obstruction/aspiration is the immediate threat.

why.A: Protect the C-spine, but the airway is the immediate killer.

stem: 30 year old man presenting after MVA” motor vehicle accident”. The patient has blood at the urethral meatus. What is the most appropriate next step?
srcNote: (Investigation of Urinary tract Problems & Renal Colic) Surgical Infections
expl: Blood at the urethral meatus = urethral injury until proven otherwise → retrograde urethrogram before any catheter.

why.C: Suprapubic if a urethrogram shows disruption and he can't void.

stem: The following are true related to flail chest except:

opts.t: It is when three or more ribs are broken in two or more places
The underlying lung is usually contused
